voiceover: You've probably sung Philippians 2 — but your English Bible hides its most explosive words in the Greek. Tucked into a prison letter is a passage that reads like a song. Scholars call it the Carmen Christi — the Song of Christ — and most think Paul is quoting something older than his letter, sung within a generation of the cross. Word one: morphe theou — the form of God. Not a costume. The same word describes the form of a servant he truly became — so the form of God is just as real. Word two: harpagmos — the reading most scholars now take: equality with God he already had, and refused to exploit. Word three: ekenosen — he emptied himself. Not of his deity. He emptied himself by adding humanity — remaining what he was, becoming what he was not. Word four: the name above every name — Kyrios, the Lord, the divine name itself. Paul takes Isaiah 45, where God swears 'to me every knee shall bow' — and applies it to Jesus. This is Jesus placed inside the identity of the one God — what Richard Bauckham calls a Christology of divine identity. The worship of Jesus as God is not a late invention. The first Christians did not argue Jesus into godhood. They sang it. Jesus is Lord — to the glory of God the Father.
